Thank you Mayor Block and City Council. My name is Darrell Dawson, manager of the development review section with the city's planning and development development. I'll be presenting the first three public hearings tonight.

So this public hearing is to consider an application from Kavita and Pram Sharma. For discretionary use approval to develop a daycare center for up to 20 children at any one time at 440. Evergreen Boulevard in the Evergreen neighborhood.

The site is showing on the screen highlighted on the left image and on the right is the site plan that is actually attached to the report. This site is zone R1A low-density residential district and a daycare center is considered a discretionary use in this zoning district.
As background, this site is currently developed as a one unit dwelling and the applicants who own the property do operate a residential daycare out of this home.
Now a residential daycare is a daycare center that provides for a maximum of 12 people under care at any one time and is considered a permitted use in the zoning district.

What the applicants are looking to do is increase the number of persons under care from 12 to 20. And that expansion changes the use from a residential daycare to a daycare center, which requires the discretionary use approval.

The proposed daycare center would remain as accessory to the existing one end dwelling and would be operated by one of the residents and they'd have two additional staff coming into assist with the operation.
So notification of this application was originally sent in March of last year to property owners within 150 meters of the site and emailed to the ward counselor and community association.
Notice was also posted on the cities engage page. We did receive 10 correspondence from that engagement all with concerns related to capacity.

The location of the site in proximity to the intersection transit stop and community mailboxes and the impact drop off and pick up what have on on those spots increase in traffic, garbage and recycling concerns and snow on the roadways impacting parking.
Following this feedback, the applicants did revise their original proposal, which was at 24 individuals and brought it down to 20 people under care to try and address neighbor concerns.

The administration then sent out revised notice in June of last year back out to 150 meters from there. We did receive seven correspondence with concerns and from there we did look to hold a public engagement meeting.
Now that meeting was not held until February of this year and at that meeting, administration and the applicant were there to answer questions about the application and the process.
Two individuals did show up that note of general concerns with the application.
So through a review, consideration was given to the comments received through the consultation process.
The proximity of other discretion uses the location on the block and the application detail such as on site parking provided and capacity of the daycare.
We did note that the applicant has revised their application down from 24 to 20 to work to address neighbor concerns.

Next slide, please. The official community plan represents Saskatoon's collective long-term vision.
It guides the city's physical, environmental, economic, social, and cultural development.

The proposed amendments are direct outcome of the city center and district plan, which was approved by City Council in September of 2024.
The plan underscores the city's commitment to maintaining and enhancing downtown and presents a vision in strategic initiatives to support and shape the city center.
It includes direction and projects for enhancing public realm, creating new plaza and park spaces, as well as shaping the land use policy for downtown.

We are now at the stage of updating the official community plan to reflect and support the vision and align our overarching policy within the official community plan with the downtown plan.
Future work will include zoning bylaw amendments for the downtown zoning districts, as well as potential for specialized zoning district for the entertainment district. Next slide, please.
The proposed amendments tonight include changes to map four, which is our land use map to reflect both current and future downtown park spaces.

The park land use designation was introduced in our official community plan in 2020, and since then administration has been applying the park designation through amendments to current and plan park areas, so that these areas are accurately represented on the land use map. Next slide, please.
Map two is proposed to be updated to reflect the distinct downtown districts that make up the collective of downtown.

The revised map is informed by current land uses, but also provides aspiration for these areas and highlight broader goals for each district and how land use contributes to both urban design and the character identity of each area. Next slide, please.
Map two also introduces the proposed active use core shown in the dark gray lines along street frontages. This replaces the current retail core, which is depicted in red on this slide.
The retail core was originally established to prioritize retail and service uses on the ground floor to support vibrant pedestrian activity in the downtown.

Reframing this as the active use core continues to highlight this area as the downtown's commercial heart, but it does expand the types of acceptable ground floor uses, recognizing that various uses can contribute to street level animation.
Changes to the boundaries are proposed as well, adding and removing certain site frontages, and these changes better reflect current conditions and future aspirations.
Because the retail core is currently linked to a zoning by-law regulation requiring a portion of ground floor space to be used for retail or services.
A related zoning by-law amendment is proposed as well to ensure consistency by updating the terminology to match the active use core. Next slide, please.

The OCP does have existing policies to promote a quality pedestrian environment in the downtown, and the plan recommended strengthening this further by prohibiting and closed pedestrian bridges over streets in the downtown.
These bridges have been shown in other North American cities to detract from street level activity, reduced pedestrian animation, and negatively impact safety perceptions.
And since the adoption of the old 2013 city center plan, the city's administrative position has been to not support these types of structures within our downtown, and the proposed amendment formally.

And beds that into policy. Reinforcing a commitment to a people-focused streets in the downtown. Next slide, please. New policy is also proposed for single purpose surface parking lots in the downtown.
